base_text: A man becomes homeless after losing his job, and struggles to recover.

variants.perspective: the person experiencing it, first person
variants.text: After the warehouse laid me off, the money ran out fast. I fell behind on rent, and within two months the landlord had me evicted. I ended up sleeping in doorways and under the bridge by the station. The cold and the lack of sleep wore me down until I was sick most of the time. Eventually I found a bed at a shelter, but no one will hire you when you can't give them an address.

David's case is common: a sudden layoff, no savings, and rent far higher than his benefits could cover, so eviction was almost inevitable. Once he was on the street his physical and mental health declined quickly. We got him into an emergency shelter, but the real trap is that without a fixed address he can't open a bank account or pass a job check, which keeps him homeless.

variants.perspective: his sister, family view (omits the job details)
variants.text: We had drifted apart, and I did not realise how bad things had got until someone told me he was living rough. He had always struggled with his moods, and being out there made it far worse. I keep thinking that if he had called me before he lost the flat, none of it would have happened.

variants.perspective: a shopkeeper passing by, surface view with a contested assumption
variants.text: There is a man who sits outside my shop most days now. People assume he drinks or takes something and that is why he is on the street, but honestly I do not know his story. He looks unwell and tired, and he is polite enough.

When David came into the shelter he was underweight and had a nasty cough we had to get treated. We sorted him a hot meal and a bed, and we have been helping him write a CV and use the shelter's address for job applications. He is desperate to work; the hard part is getting an employer to look past the gap and the missing address.

Stories like this follow a familiar chain: stagnant wages and mass layoffs collide with soaring rents, pushing people from housing insecurity into outright homelessness. Once on the street, health deteriorates and pressure shifts onto emergency shelters and hospitals, while the lack of an address makes re-employment nearly impossible, so the cycle sustains itself.
